title: Count Originals Behind One Sticky Key
statement:
Someone typed a word on a keyboard with a sticky key. While typing, they held a key down too long at most once, so one letter of the intended word may have come out repeated extra times. The extra copies sit right next to the letter they belong to.

You get what appeared on screen, word. Return how many different intended words could have produced it. The screen text itself counts if nothing stuck.

examples.why: Nothing stuck: "abbccc". The b stuck once: "abccc". The c stuck once or twice: "abbcc" or "abbc".
No letter is repeated, so nothing can have stuck.
"aabb", "abb" or "aab". Only one key stuck, so "ab" is not possible; multiplying run lengths (2 · 2 = 4) overcounts.

constraints: word has only lowercase English letters
hints: Split the word into runs of the same letter. Where could the stuck key have been?
A run of length L could have been typed as 1, 2, …, L copies. If it is the run that stuck, how many choices does that give, not counting "nothing stuck"?
Each run of length L adds L − 1 options, and the untouched word adds 1. That is 1 plus the number of positions where a letter equals the one before it.

explain.intuition:
Group the word into runs of equal letters. If the sticky key belonged to a run of length L, the intended run had 1 to L − 1 copies: L − 1 different originals. Different runs give different originals, and "nothing stuck" adds one more.

The sum of L − 1 over all runs is just the number of positions where a letter equals the letter before it. So the answer is 1 + that count. Because only one key stuck, the choices per run add up; they do not multiply.
steps: Set count = 1 for the case where nothing stuck.
For each i from 1 to n − 1, add 1 when word[i] = word[i − 1].
pitfalls: Multiplying the run lengths, which counts several keys sticking at once.
Forgetting the case where nothing stuck, which is off by one.
Counting the same letter in separate runs together: in "abba" the two a's are not a run.

solutions.title: Build every candidate
solutions.idea: For each run and each shorter length, build the shortened string; collect them in a set together with the word.

solutions.title: Count equal neighbors
solutions.idea: Each run of length L contributes L − 1 originals, which is the number of equal adjacent pairs inside it. Add 1 for no sticking.

followups: Several keys may stick, and you know the intended word had at least k letters. How do you count now? (Hint: DP over runs.)
Return the list of possible originals in lexicographic order.
lcTitle: Find the Original Typed String I
